summary: The note describes the growing integration of coding and computational thinking into school curricula, arguing it supports academic success and could close achievement gaps. It covers the research case, cross-subject application, the digital divide, educator training, portfolio-based assessment, and early longitudinal findings, while acknowledging significant obstacles ahead.
one_line: Schools are integrating coding and computational thinking into curricula, facing challenges in equity, teacher training, and assessment, with early research showing benefits.
key_facts: Since September 2023, many schools have implemented coding classes and computational exercises as a core part of the curriculum.

Jeanette Stevenson, an educational researcher, published a study in October 2023 arguing that coding education prepares students for job markets and enhances abstract thinking and methodical problem-solving.
Data cited by Stevenson suggests students exposed to coding from a young age perform better in mathematics and logic-based subjects.
Michael Tan, a curriculum advisor, has promoted computational thinking since September 2024 and argues it should not be siloed within computer science courses.
Tan says applying computational thinking in history, literature, or physical education gives students a more holistic and enriched educational experience.
A major concern is that students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds may lack equal access to technology, widening the academic achievement gap.
In December 2023, nonprofit 'Code for All' launched partnerships with schools in underprivileged areas to provide resources and training.
Sandra Ramirez, director of 'Code for All', says every child, irrespective of background, should have the opportunity to learn these skills.
A teacher training program led by Derek Li has had over 2,000 teachers participate since its inception in January 2024.
Derek Li stresses teaching teachers not just how to code, but how to teach coding, building confidence that trickles down to students.
Jane Park, an assessment expert, advocates portfolio-based assessment, evaluating a student's body of work rather than a single test score.
Gregory Huang is conducting longitudinal studies; preliminary findings released in February 2025 suggest improvements in computational skills, collaboration, communication, and critical thinking.
